articles.title: 2026 is the year of social media’s legal reckoning
articles.summary: Meta, Snap, TikTok, and YouTube are set to face several trials this year over claims that they designed their products in ways that harmed kids.
articles.body: Over the next year, top social media executives are expected to take the witness stand to defend their companies from an avalanche of claims about their failure to protect kids. The first of many trials is set to begin this month in California, when Meta, TikTok, and YouTube face claims that tech addiction harmed a teenager’s mental health. This case is just the tip of the legal iceberg. It kicks off one of two sets of so-called bellwether trials, where judges will hear a selection of cases that represent similar claims, whose outcomes will likely inform settlement amounts for the remaining cases. There are still thousands more cases behind them. They’re significant both for managing the rare feat of overcoming Section 230 objections that protect online platforms from liability for their users’ speech to reach a full trial phase, and because of the evidence they could reveal regarding what social media platforms knew and did — or didn’t do — about the harms they could cause kids. “When we started doing this work, it was a given that we could not even get past a motion to dismiss,” Matthew Bergman, the founder of the Social Media Victims Law Center, which represents the plaintiff in the first of the trials taking place this month, said at a recent briefing. “The simple fact that a social media company is going to have to stand trial before a jury and account for its design decisions is unprecedented in American jurisprudence. This has never happened before.” All of the companies named in the cases — Meta, Google’s YouTube, TikTok, and Snap — say they have robust policies to keep kids safe online. “Providing young people with a safer, healthier experience has always been core to our work,” YouTube spokesperson José Castañeda said in a statement. “The allegations in these complaints are simply not true.” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone pointed to the company’s recent blog post, which said that blaming social media companies for teens’ mental health issues “oversimplifies a serious issue.” Stone added, “We strongly disagree with these allegations and are confident the evidence will show our longstanding commitment to supporting young people.” TikTok did not provide comment by publication time, but has defended its trust and safety measures in the past. Snap settled with the plaintiff in the first case going to trial, and Snap spokesperson Monique Bellamy said in a statement that “The Parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner.” In the trials, plaintiffs are seeking monetary damages and changes to social platforms. But no matter the outcome, new revelations from these trials could create more pressure on both the companies and lawmakers to enact changes. How the bellwether cases work Thousands of individuals, school districts, and state attorneys general from across the country have filed suit against social media companies, which they allege harmed teens’ mental health. Since the cases hit on similar themes requiring similar discovery and legal procedures, they were consolidated to more efficiently manage the caseload. These groupings of cases are known as the Judicial Council Coordination Proceedings (JCCP) for the state system and Multidistrict Litigation (MDL) for the federal system. Within each grouping, a subgroup of bellwether cases will be tried first, and are roughly representative of the whole group’s claims. When one bellwether concludes, they will move on to the next. The idea is that by trying a sampling of cases, parties will have a sense for how juries will tend to rule on certain kinds of claims and the amount of damages they might be awarded, which can inform the terms of a broader settlement. (This is distinct from a class action lawsuit, where a group of similarly situated parties join a single lawsuit and the outcome applies to all of them equally.) Additionally, evidence from earlier trials can be referenced in later ones — so high-profile tech CEOs, for instance, are likely to only testify once. Individual cases or defendants may choose to settle at any point, but ultimately the parties will likely try to reach a global settlement that resolves the remaining, larger pile of cases — similar to what’s happened in litigation over the opioid epidemic. While several defendants may be facing similar claims during the trials, each company will have an opportunity to make its own case, and a jury might find some liable, but not others. California state court cases The first of the social media product liability cases is set to go to trial Tuesday in a state court in Los Angeles in front of Judge Carolyn Kuhl. The case involves an unnamed teen identified as K.G.M., now 19 years old, who says she experienced an addiction to several social media apps that resulted in other mental health issues. The week before the trial, Snap reached a settlement, but the trial will still include Meta, TikTok, and YouTube as defendants, as of Monday. Top company executives, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, are expected to testify, as is K.G.M. The trial is expected to last at least six weeks. Once it concludes, the court will move down the list of an initial three bellwether cases. Federal court cases The federal cases consolidated into the MDL in the Northern District of California include cases brought by school districts, individual plaintiffs, and state attorneys general. The first six bellwether cases will represent school districts across the country, essentially arguing that the designs of social media platforms have kept their students compulsively using them, leading the school districts to expend resources on mental health and other issues. The board of education in Breathitt County, Kentucky, will be the first to try its case beginning in June before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland. This is the litigation from which a trove of internal social media company documents has already come to light, revealing, for example, that a user experience researcher at Meta allegedly compared Instagram to a drug. The internal communications are just an example of the kinds of evidence that could come out in the various trials in the months to come. There is a significant hearing slated for Monday, where the judge will hear arguments on a motion for summary judgment. The results of that hearing will determine what issues are allowed to be included in the trials later this year. New Mexico v. Meta Beginning February 2nd, Meta will face a trial brought by the New Mexico attorney general for allegedly creating a “marketplace for predators in search of children” on its platforms. To make it to trial, the case notably overcame arguments from Meta that Section 230 should shield it from the litigation. To test their claims, the New Mexico attorney general’s office created accounts on Meta’s services posing as kids or parents seeking to traffic them and said they found that the service quickly surfaced the accounts to strangers, garnering largely adult male followings. Using the underage decoy accounts, the government arrested several suspected child predators who the AG’s office said solicited sex from the accounts. “While New Mexico makes sensationalist, irrelevant and distracting arguments, we’re focused on demonstrating our longstanding commitment to supporting young people,” Stone, the Meta spokesperson, said in a statement.

articles.title: Over the next decade, the U.S. Treasury will spend $20 trillion in interest on the national debt—$200 billion a month by 2036
articles.summary: "The challenge for me is I can't say for sure what is the deadline, when do we need to act. That's something members want to know, and we don't know, which i...
articles.body:
As the largest economy on earth, the U.S. government can afford to borrow staggering amounts of money without lenders batting an eyelid. However, projections for the Treasury's revenues versus its expected spending over the next decade would give even the most optimistic budget doves pause. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) this week released its projections of federal receipts and expenditures in the national income for 2026-2036. Economists are used to seeing eye-watering figures when it comes to the U.S. budget: The nation is currently running a $40 trillion debt burden and has yet to face the fiscal crisis predicted by debt hawks for many years. However, with the trust fund for Social Security due to run out in a little over seven years, and Medicare to go insolvent in six and a half years, budget questions are pushing further up the agendas of both politicians and the public.

The CBO's projections for government spending—irrespective of which party is in power—are only likely to add fuel to those concerns. Between 2026 and 2036, the CBO's report suggests that $20.1 trillion will be spent on interest payments servicing the national debt. That is both on the current debt burden of $40 trillion, as well as the deficits adding to that pile over the next decade.

In 2026, the U.S. Treasury paid $1.2 trillion in interest on the debt, the CBO noted. By 2036, this increases to a little under $2.5 trillion a year—or $200 billion a month.

Putting that figure into context, the expected spend on the defense of the nation is $1.1 trillion by 2036, meaning roughly double that figure will be spent servicing borrowing.

Despite pressure to reduce deficits—with proposals to target budget shortfalls at 3% of GDP rather than the current 6% to 7%—the CBO expects the gap between revenues and expenditures to widen over the next decade. The Treasury has confirmed that the fiscal year 2026 deficit was $2 trillion. The CBO projects it will widen to more than $3 trillion by 2036. The total budget shortfall between this year and a decade from now is $25.6 trillion.

A major driver of the continued need to borrow is the increase in social benefits. The U.S., like many of its Western peers, has an aging population, meaning more people will stop working and will likely rely on state social and health services. In 2026, the spending stood at $3.7 trillion; by 2036, it will likely stand at $6.1 trillion, the CBO reports.

Policymakers have cycled through a range of ideas on how to address budget concerns, with the current administration suggesting tariffs could have been a gamechanger in rebalancing.

articles.title: Professora é afastada após post sobre filhos de eleitores de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Docente do município de Melgaço teve processo de rescisão contratual por justa causa iniciado pela prefeitura após a divulgação das mensagens nas redes sociais.
articles.summary: A prefeitura de Melgaço afastou a professora Marinalva do Carmo Gomes por publicações que incitam violência sexual contra filhos de eleitores do presidente Lula.
articles.body:
Professora compartilha mensagens com incentivo a violência sexual contra filhos de eleitores de Lula no Pará. — Foto: Reprodução / Redes sociais

Uma professora de Melgaço , no Marajó, foi afastada do cargo após publicar mensagens nas redes sociais com conteúdo de violência sexual contra filhos de eleitores do presidente reeleito Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). O caso foi confirmado ao g1 nesta quinta-feira (29) pela Secretaria Municipal de Educação (Semed) do Município.

As mensagens publicadas pela professora Marinalva do Carmo Gomes podem configurar conduta criminosa, com enquadramentos na legislação penal brasileira, e também violam os direitos de proteção integral garantidos pelo Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA).

Após a repercussão do caso, Marinalva pediu desculpas e lamentou "profundamente o ocorrido". Por meio de nota nas redes, ela disse estar arrependida. "Reconheço que me excedi em minhas palavras e que posso ter magoado e ofendido algumas pessoas", disse - ( veja a nota completa ao final).

Nas publicações, a professora usou palavras de baixo calão e expressões agressivas para incentivar a violência sexual contra crianças por causa do posicionamento político dos pais.

O Sindicato dos Trabalhadores em Educação Pública do Pará (Sintepp), em Melgaço, divulgou uma nota de repúdio às declarações. A entidade classificou as manifestações como inadmissíveis e afirmou que elas não representam os profissionais da educação do município.

Segundo o sindicato da categoria, as mensagens contrariam os direitos das crianças e dos adolescentes, ferem a integridade de crianças, jovens e famílias e violam princípios constitucionais, o ECA e o Código de Ética do Magistério.

O Sintepp também cobrou uma apuração rigorosa e a adoção de medidas legais pelas autoridades competentes, incluindo o Conselho Tutelar, o Ministério Público, a Secretaria Municipal de Educação e os órgãos de segurança.

A docente trabalhava em regime de contrato temporário na Escola Municipal de Ensino Fundamental Gervásio Bandeira. De acordo com a Semed, foi aberto um processo de rescisão do contrato por justa causa.

Em nota, a secretaria disse que "diante da gravidade dos fatos e da legítima indignação da população, a profissional foi afastada de suas atividades laborativas, enquanto são adotados os procedimentos administrativos e legais necessários à análise da rescisão de seu contrato".

"Reafirmamos que manifestações dessa natureza são incompatíveis com os princípios e as responsabilidades que devem orientar a atuação dos profissionais da educação", conclui a nota.

Por que a conduta da professora é crime?

Segundo o advogado criminalista Rodrigo Costa, as mensagens podem "configurar condutas de extrema gravidade perante o ordenamento jurídico brasileiro", como incitação ao crime, apologia de crime, crimes contra a honra e conflito de discriminação de procedência, implicações administrativas e funcionais (previstos no Estatuto do Servidor).

"As supostas declarações transcendem o debate político e a liberdade de opinião, ingressando na esfera da criminalidade comum e da infração funcional grave. Ela pode estar sujeita a responder penalmente perante à Justiça, além de sofrer o banimento do serviço público e do magistério por meio de processo de destituição de cargo", explicou.

O g1 entrou em contato com a Polícia Civil , o Ministério Público do Pará (MPPA) e o Ministério Público Federal (MPF), que informaram não ter sido acionados sobre o caso.

"Eu, Marinalva do Carmo Gomes, professora da Escola Gervásio Bandeira, venho, por meio desta declaração, pedir sinceras desculpas por palavras que falei em um momento de muita emoção e que não deveria ter dito.

Reconheço que me excedi em minhas palavras e que posso ter magoado e ofendido algumas pessoas. Por isso, venho pedir perdão a cada uma delas, especialmente à equipe da Escola Gervásio Bandeira e à Secretaria Municipal de Educação de Melgaço.

Quero expressar meu arrependimento e dizer que lamento profundamente o ocorrido. Peço desculpas a todos que se sentiram ofendidos pelas minhas palavras. Comprometo-me a ter mais cuidado com minhas atitudes e palavras, para que uma situação como essa não volte a acontecer.

Espero que minhas desculpas sejam recebidas com compreensão e respeito. Reafirmo meu pedido de perdão a todos."

articles.title: Bluesky blocks links to leaked DHS employee data as government seeks takedowns | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The social networking site is facing criticism for blocking access to the site, which identifies thousands of ICE agents and other employees working for Homeland Security.
articles.body:
Following a sizable leak of personnel data about employees who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, social network Bluesky is now blocking its users from accessing a nonprofit’s website that hosts the leaked dataset.

Users reported that the links to nonprofit transparency collective DDoSecrets were marked as “malicious” soon after TechCrunch and other media outlets broke the news that Homeland Security had been hacked.

TechCrunch reported on Wednesday that a hacker obtained over 40,000 user account records from Homeland Security’s login system, including the names and contact information, such as work-issued phone numbers and email addresses, of employees and agents working for its various agencies like Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The data included information that was similar to that on an employee’s business card. DDoSecrets, which publishes leaked datasets in the public interest, also made the hacked data publicly available. Researchers who are investigating abuses by the Trump administration say that the data will be invaluable for seeking records from the government under public records laws.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch on Wednesday that it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.”

In a statement, Bluesky chief operating officer Rose Wang told TechCrunch: “Our Community Guidelines protect people’s safety and privacy by prohibiting the unauthorized sharing of personal information and other content that could pose safety risks. Because the files include the email addresses and phone numbers of individuals, shared without their authorization, we are blocking links to the dataset.”

“When deciding between blocking a link and removing individual posts, we chose to block the links to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary,” said Wang.

In a post on Bluesky, Wang said that the company plans to change the wording on the block message. “We should have changed the wording last night. Changes incoming shortly,” said Wang.

DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best told TechCrunch that while Bluesky’s terms of service prohibit sharing home addresses and personal contact information, Best said that neither of these is in the leaked dataset.

“The data contains professional contact information for government employees at a time when the public interest in that exact information has never been higher. By requiring the public to provide it for [Freedom of Information Act] requests, the government has made that exact information a crucial piece of the transparency channels they want the public to engage in,” said Best.

Homeland Security sends takedown notices

Best told TechCrunch that a website hosting a searchable copy of the stolen data was taken down by its domain registrar, effectively knocking the website offline for now.

A search site , dubbed Icepick, made by journalist maia arson crimew no longer loads as of Thursday morning. An internet record associated with the domain says it has been placed on “serverHold,” which generally means that the domain registrar locked or closed the domain for some reason.

Homeland Security filed a takedown notice via a security vendor called ZeroFox, which has authority to act on the department’s behalf until 2028 to seek the removal of data from the internet. TechCrunch has seen a copy of the takedown notice for the search site, which asks that the domain registrar “stop serving the personal contact and location data of individuals who did not consent to its publication.”

CentralNic, which hosts the domain name, did not respond to a request for comment from TechCrunch about the takedown or whether it was instructed to do so by a government demand. ZeroFox also did not respond to a request for comment.

The Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up regarding the takedown notice affecting Icepick’s website.

Crimew also made a locally hosted version of the data, allowing anyone to access it on their own computer.

articles.title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't.
articles.body:
French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month .

The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems.

Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.”

The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes.

Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3.

The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site.

“Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.”

The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API.

Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves.

“Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said.

Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem.

While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide [this same] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.”

Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting.

“We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said.

articles.title: Utah charges Kalshi and its CEO with illegally promoting online gambling
articles.summary: Utah has filed criminal charges against Kalshi, accusing it of illegally promoting online gambling.
articles.body: Utah has filed criminal charges against Kalshi and its executives, accusing the prediction market of breaking anti-gambling laws, as reported by The Salt Lake Tribune and the Associated Press. The state has filed 14 charges against Kalshi, as well as CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara, including 12 counts of illegally promoting online gambling. The move marks an escalation in a nationwide battle against prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket. Utah has already sued Kalshi over claims that it’s operating illegally in the state, joining several other states, including New York, Nevada, New Mexico, Washington, Connecticut, and others, in taking legal action against the company. New York and Kentucky have sued Polymarket as well. In March, Arizona became the first state to file criminal charges against Kalshi, but a federal judge later blocked its case. In the backdrop of these legal battles, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is fighting state-level attempts to regulate prediction markets, arguing that it has “exclusive jurisdiction” over the platforms. States recently netted wins with two federal appeals courts ruling against Kalshi and Polymarket’s bid to fight state-level oversight. However, the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in April that the CFTC has the exclusive authority to regulate prediction markets in New Jersey, which recently asked the Supreme Court to take up its case. Kalshi says Utah’s charges are a “crazy overreach” in a statement provided to the Associated Press, adding: “We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona.”

articles.title: FTC seeking information from Walmart, JetBlue, others on pricing
articles.summary: The Federal Trade Commission has ordered nine U.S. companies to turn over information on how they use consumers' personal data to set prices.
articles.body:
Oct. 29 (UPI) -- The Federal Trade Commission has ordered nine U.S. companies, including Walmart and Uber, to turn over information on how they use consumers' personal data to set prices and gig worker pay.

The companies, which also include Delta Airlines, United Airlines, JetBlue Airlines, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart and Target, were named by the agency on Wednesday, following probes of "surveillance pricing" and lawsuits alleging consumers have been charged different prices based on purchase histories.

The FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said it will "scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service."

For rideshare and delivery services, the FTC said it will examine how those companies determine worker pay. Offers that drivers received may depend on opaque formulas, possibly involving data such as phone usage or a driver's history of accepting offers previously.

Legislation has been introduced in several states to bar surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels that could be used to set various prices for shoppers based on their habits and online information.

The FTC's announcement follows a lawsuit it and 20 states filed against Dollar General on Monday, alleging the discount retailer charges consumers more than advertised. The Goodlettsville, Tenn.-based company has repeatedly mislabeled prices and overcharged customers despite corporate being aware of the issues, the lawsuit claims.

articles.title: One issue, different bills: Energy costs shape key midterm races
articles.summary: Diesel prices are squeezing Midwest farmers, while homeowners in the Northeast are worried about costly heating oil.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) – Higher energy costs have helped make affordability a top issue in the 2026 midterms , but voters aren’t all worried about the same bills.

Diesel prices are squeezing Midwest farmers , while homeowners in the Northeast face soaring heating oil costs . Others in data center hotspots like Texas and Ohio are worried about their electricity bills .

Democrats have tried to tie those issues to President Trump , pointing to the war in Iran and his embrace of AI . As of Wednesday, Decision Desk HQ gave Democrats an 80 percent chance of winning the House and a 58 percent chance of controlling the Senate .

Some Republicans have called for an end to the Iran war, while others have blamed high prices on Ukraine’s war with Russia and Democrats’ energy policies.

To win the Senate, Democrats will have to break through on Republican turf . Of the Cook Political Report’s seven toss-ups , five are in states Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Diesel prices are more than 70 percent higher than a year ago amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and farmers across America’s heartland are feeling the pain .

In Iowa, diesel averaged $6.14 a gallon on Wednesday, an increase of $2.50 from a year earlier, according to AAA . Kansas has seen a similar jump.

The surge comes at a particularly bad time for farmers, who rely on diesel to power tractors and combines during harvest season. It’s also become a political problem for Republicans, who are now facing unexpectedly close races in states Trump won handily in 2024.

Republican Ashley Hinson is running neck and neck with Democrat Josh Turek for Iowa’s open Senate seat, while Democrat Adam Hamilton has gained ground on Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas.

Trump has tried to shore up rural support, recently announcing an $8 billion “harvest fuel relief program” aimed at offsetting farmers’ diesel costs with one-time payments.

The Iowa Farmers Union called the move a “Band-Aid response” that “doesn’t fix the problem.” After years without endorsing a federal candidate, the organization is backing Democrats in all five of Iowa’s congressional races.

Other farm groups are supporting Republicans. The Iowa Corn Growers Association has endorsed Hinson, while the Kansas Farm Bureau’s political arm is backing Marshall.

Data center expansion fuels utility bill anxiety

Most Americans don’t want AI data centers in their communities, and concerns about higher utility bills are part of the reason why.

The issue has taken center stage in Texas, where Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is seeking a fourth term, and Democrats are hoping to flip a competitive Senate seat .

Texas is expected to overtake Virginia as the world’s largest data center market by 2030, according to JLL , but the boom has drawn pushback.

A new University of Houston poll found nearly 80 percent of Texas voters support limits on data center construction, while 76 percent expect the projects to raise electricity costs in communities where they’re built.

Abbott, who called the state the “epicenter of AI development” as recently as last November, has since tapped the brakes, ordering a pause on environmental permits for data centers while officials complete an audit.

Data centers have also become a flashpoint in Senate races in Ohio and Michigan, two contests that could decide which party controls the chamber.

In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers supports a one-year pause on new data center construction while Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s “ terms of engagement ” proposal calls for data centers to cover their own energy costs and protect local water resources.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown has criticized Republican Sen. Jon Husted for promoting data centers during his time as lieutenant governor. As a senator, Husted introduced legislation aimed at keeping data centers’ energy costs off household bills.

New Englanders brace for higher heating bills

Winter is right around the corner, and keeping warm will be more expensive for the roughly 4.8 million U.S. households that rely on heating oil .

Heating oil ​prices have soared to $6.23 per gallon nationally, up from around $3.60 a year ago, according to the Energy Information Administration . Like diesel, heating oil has been hit by global supply disruptions linked to the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars.

Higher costs will hit especially hard in the Northeast, which is home to 82 percent of U.S. households that use heating oil as their primary heating fuel.

In Maine, where roughly half of households use heating oil to warm their homes, rising prices have become a major issue in the Senate race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson .

Jackson has blamed the increase on the Iran war and criticized Collins’ voting record on the conflict. Collins, who’s running for a sixth term, said earlier this month that she had urged the Trump administration to use “every tool available” to increase supply and bring down energy costs.

Last week, the Energy Department said it would make up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil available from the government’s Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve in an effort to bring down prices.

Collins praised the decision , saying it will “make a real difference for Maine homeowners as they prepare for winter.”

William O’Neil, an analyst at S&P Global Energy, told The New York Times that “the volume is too small relative to consumption to significantly change supply.”

articles.title: Hegseth, Mullin call Trump’s arch a ‘generational defense opportunity’
articles.summary: President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch would be a “generational defense opportunity,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin have argued in court declarations. Critics have dismissed Trump’s attempts to link the arch to national security needs as a smokescreen to push through a divisive construction project. In filings submitted to a federal…
articles.body:
President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch would be a “generational defense opportunity,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin have argued in court declarations.

Critics have dismissed Trump’s attempts to link the arch to national security needs as a smokescreen to push through a divisive construction project.

In filings submitted to a federal court on Wednesday, Hegseth and Mullin said the arch intended for erection between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial was needed to keep the U.S. safe from drone attacks and to serve as a base for snipers.

“The arch is a generational national defense opportunity to mitigate these evolving threats,” Hegseth said, adding that the arch’s proposed 250-foot height would give a “significant elevation advantage” as it could enhance “lines of sight from both sensors and personnel.”

“It will be utilized as a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense,” he said.

Mullin, meanwhile, told the court the arch would “incorporate a number of features that will support national security” and could be used by the Secret Service to beef up security for senior government officials.

Both men claim the design of the arch didn’t need to be changed to convert it into a base for counter-drone operations, which would require new regulatory reviews by relevant agencies.

“The implementation of the capabilities discussed in this declaration would not require any structural modifications or alterations to the existing plans for the arch,” Hegseth said.

Trump, in his initial proposal of the arch last October, said the monument was meant to honor “me.” The administration later insisted the arch is in honor of the United States’s 250th anniversary and a tourist attraction — until last month.

The president in a September Truth Social post claimed the structure would be a “top grade Military Complex” used to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas,” as well as store “large quantities” of ammunition.

The abrupt announcement came amid opposition to the project, with Democrats and veterans groups opposing its proximity to Arlington and the disruption it will cause to burials during construction and after its completion. The project is expected to take at least three years.

Opponents of the project say Trump is abusing the national security justification, as he did with construction of the White House ballroom. The president has insisted the ballroom is necessary for national security as it will include a military complex underneath.

Trump, however, asserted the changes to the arch were being made at the “strong request” of the U.S. military.

The changes called into question whether the National Park Service’s proposals for the structure — approved in May by the heavily Trump-appointed Commission of Fine Arts — would need to be resubmitted, which would slow the project.

Final site plans for the arch do not mention the military features Trump said he would add to the project, according to documentation the Interior Department submitted to the National Capital Planning Commission.

The National Capital Planning Commission, also led by Trump allies, will ultimately give final approval, a decision slated for next week.

There is also a Friday hearing set to decide whether the White House has authority to build the arch at the intended location. The Justice Department has told the federal court that the administration could begin construction as early as Nov. 5, after the commission’s vote.

articles.title: Finnish police launch criminal probe over forest cleared for Google data center
articles.summary: Finnish police opened a criminal investigation Thursday into Google’s work on a planned data center in northern Finland after the company cleared hundreds of acres of forest without completing required environmental reviews. The investigation adds to mounting scrutiny of Google’s $1.5 billion investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure in Finland, where the company’s expansion plans have…
articles.body:
Finnish police opened a criminal investigation Thursday into Google’s work on a planned data center in northern Finland after the company cleared hundreds of acres of forest without completing required environmental reviews.

The investigation adds to mounting scrutiny of Google’s $1.5 billion investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure in Finland, where the company’s expansion plans have raised concerns over deforestation and rising energy costs.

Authorities are investigating whether Tuike Finland, a Google subsidiary, violated environmental laws while preparing a site near the northern town of Muhos. According to Finnish authorities, the company cleared and drained approximately 815 acres of forest before completing environmental impact assessments.

A spokesperson for Google told Reuters that the company would cooperate with authorities.

“We’ve partnered closely with the government and communities in Finland on infrastructure for over a decade, and are actively responding to enquiries from LVV [Finnish Supervisory Agency] and other authorities,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

“We are investigating whether the company’s ​operations have breached the water act and resulted in environmental damage,” Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen said in a statement to Reuters, adding that the company could face a corporate fine if found guilty of the violations.

The probe follows an Oct. 6 order from Finland’s environmental regulator directing Google to suspend work at two planned data center locations, Muhos and Otanmäki, until the necessary environmental requirements are met.

Environmental groups estimate that roughly 400,000 trees have been cut down across the two sites.

Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, previously apologized for the clearing but said the company had operated based on its understanding of the country’s environmental requirements.

The controversy comes as Finland seeks to establish itself as a major European hub for AI infrastructure. Google announced its $1.5 billion investment last month, with plans to develop data centers and support clean energy projects.

articles.title: Millions of students caught in California data breach
articles.summary: Educational Testing Service hackers stole millions of California student records, but families who moved out of state years ago may also be affected.
articles.body: You send your child to school expecting teachers to protect their education. You probably don't think much about what happens to their personal information after they take a standardized test. But a massive data breach in California is raising some uncomfortable questions about who has access to student records and how safely that information is stored. Hackers accessed and copied sensitive records belonging to millions of current and former California public school students. The stolen information includes home addresses, birth dates and even details about disabilities. And here's something families need to know. You could live thousands of miles from California today and still be caught up in this breach if you or your child previously attended a public school there. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. ORACLE HEALTH DATA BREACH EXPOSES NEARLY 20 MILLION PATIENTS How millions of California student records were stolen The breach involves Educational Testing Service (ETS), a nonprofit organization that works with the California Department of Education. ETS helps administer statewide student assessments and maintains information connected to those tests. According to state officials, someone gained unauthorized access to an ETS-operated secure file transfer site. Investigators determined that the attacker used a compromised login credential to enter the system. The intruder then copied files containing student information at various times between May 22 and Sept. 18, 2026. ETS discovered the suspicious activity on Sept. 25. The company disabled the affected account and took the file transfer site offline. It also brought in outside cybersecurity specialists to investigate. The company says it has since built a replacement system with stronger security controls. So far, ETS reports finding no evidence that the stolen information has been made publicly available. However, investigators have confirmed that someone accessed and copied the records. What personal information was stolen in the student data breach? The California student data breach involved far more than test scores. Depending on the student, the compromised files may contain information that could help someone identify a child or learn personal details about their family circumstances. The exposed records may include: Some records also identified whether a student qualified for programs serving children experiencing homelessness or other educational needs. Fortunately, officials say the stolen files did not contain Social Security numbers, financial account details, driver's license numbers, passwords or parent and guardian personal information. However, there is still plenty to be concerned about. Someone who knows a child's name, school and address could potentially use that information to create a convincing message that appears to come from a teacher or school administrator. Disability information also raises additional privacy concerns because those details are particularly personal. Why this California breach could affect families nationwide This is where the story gets especially troubling. Although the breach involves California's public school system, the people whose records were stolen may now live anywhere in the United States. According to the California Department of Education, the compromised information includes records covering all students enrolled during the previous three school years. However, the affected population extends beyond those students. The state also identifies a group of former students who left California public schools as far back as 2006 and whose transfers to another school were never confirmed with the department. That creates a situation many families may never have considered. Say your child attended elementary school in Los Angeles before your family relocated to Texas. Perhaps you graduated from a California public school years ago and now live in Florida. Your old student information could still be among the compromised records if it falls within the affected groups. Former students who are now adults may also be eligible for the free identity-protection services being offered. Importantly, this does not mean every student attending school outside California has been affected. In a statement to CyberGuy, ETS confirmed that no other ETS customers were affected by the incident. The concern for families elsewhere comes from their past connection to California's public schools. California has roughly 5.7 million public school students, according to reporting on the breach. Since the compromised files span multiple school years, millions of people are potentially involved. Officials have not yet released a final count of unique affected individuals. Where the student data breach investigation stands The California Department of Education and the State Board of Education are coordinating with cybersecurity specialists and other state agencies. The California Cybersecurity Integration Center is assisting with the technical investigation. Meanwhile, state officials are reviewing ETS's compliance with applicable data security requirements and its contractual obligations. In its statement to CyberGuy, ETS said, "We have implemented additional safeguards, including enhanced monitoring, strengthened access controls, and further third-party review of our security practices." ETS says it continues monitoring for signs that the stolen information has surfaced publicly. For families, the unresolved question is what happens to the copied information next. Even without evidence of a public leak, sensitive student records in unauthorized hands create a privacy risk that deserves continued attention. A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO? How to find out if your information was exposed ETS began notifying affected students and families on October 16, 2026. The state expects notifications to continue through early November. Letters and emails will explain the incident and identify the types of information involved. They will also include instructions for accessing complimentary identity-protection services. However, here's an important warning. Not receiving a notification does not necessarily mean your information is safe. Some former students may have outdated contact information on file. Families who are concerned should visit the official California ETS incident webpage. It contains frequently asked questions and links to breach notifications available in 27 languages. You can also call the incident assistance line at 833-931-8488, Monday through Friday, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pacific Time. Affected students can get two years of free identity protection ETS is offering affected current and former students 24 months of free identity theft protection. Parents or legal guardians can enroll eligible children under 18, while adults, including former students, can enroll themselves. The services are designed to help monitor for potential identity theft and provide assistance if someone misuses their personal information. The enrollment deadline is March 19, 2027. Eligible minors who turn 18 before March 19, 2029 may also qualify for adult coverage using the activation code provided in their notification. Enrollment is free, and no credit card is required. Identity restoration assistance is also available to eligible individuals for 24 months from their notification date, even without enrolling in monitoring services. For complete eligibility details and enrollment instructions, visit the California Department of Education's official incident webpage at at cde.ca.gov/nr/in/ets-incident.asp. How to protect your child after the California student data breach Even without stolen passwords or financial account numbers, student records deserve serious attention. Here are practical steps I recommend taking if your family may be affected. 1. Verify the breach notification before responding Scammers frequently use real data breaches as an excuse to send fraudulent emails. A message claiming to come from ETS or Experian could direct you to a fake enrollment website. Instead of clicking an unexpected link, open your browser and visit the official California Department of Education incident page. Follow the verified instructions from there. 2. Consider identity theft protection Eligible families should take advantage of the 24 months of free identity-protection services being offered following this breach. Follow the enrollment instructions in your official notification and keep a copy for your records. No credit card is required. For additional protection, consider an identity theft protection service which offers identity monitoring, alerts about suspicious activity and access to restoration specialists if identity theft occurs. Some services also offer paid family plans that can cover children, making it an option for parents concerned about protecting their family's personal information over the long term. Coverage and benefits vary by plan. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com. 3. Consider freezing your child's credit One of the strongest steps you can take against certain forms of identity theft is placing a security freeze on a child's credit file. The Federal Trade Commission says parents and legal guardians can request a free credit freeze for children under 16. Teenagers ages 16 and 17 can request their own freezes. Contact Equifax, Experian and TransUnion separately. Each bureau has its own process for handling minors. A freeze can make it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts using a child's identity. However, it cannot prevent every form of fraud. 4. Watch for suspicious school-related messages Pay closer attention to unexpected emails or text messages claiming to involve school records. A scammer with access to personal details could make a fraudulent communication seem unusually credible. For example, someone might claim that your child's testing account requires immediate verification. Before responding, contact the school using a phone number you already trust. Avoid sharing personal information through unexpected links or attachments. Consider using strong antivirus software on your family's devices. It can help detect malicious links, suspicious downloads and malware hidden in fake school notifications. While it cannot recover stolen student information, it adds another layer of protection against scammers who may try to exploit the breach. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com 5. Remove your family's personal information from the internet Scammers can use information found online to build a more detailed profile of you or your family. That's why I recommend considering a personal data removal service. These services can help remove personal information from data broker websites that collect and sell details such as names, addresses and phone numbers. While these services cannot retrieve information stolen in this breach, they can help reduce how much additional information is publicly available. If you're concerned about your child's information, check whether the service offers protection for minors before signing up. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 6. Check for signs of identity theft Adults who may have been affected can review their credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or suspicious activity. Visit AnnualCreditReport.com to obtain free reports from the three major credit bureaus. Parents should also watch for unexpected bills or collection notices addressed to their children. Those can be warning signs that someone has misused a minor's identity. If you discover evidence of identity theft, report it through IdentityTheft.gov . The FTC provides a recovery plan to help you address fraudulent accounts and document the problem. 7. Ask what information your child's school retains You can also contact your child's school district to better understand how it handles student records. Ask what information outside contractors receive and how long they retain it. Schools may have legal obligations to maintain certain records. Still, parents can ask about retention policies and security safeguards. This conversation is worthwhile regardless of where your family lives. Kurt's key takeaways I've covered plenty of data breaches over the years, but this one bothers me because we're talking about children who had no choice about handing over their information. They went to school, took required tests and trusted the adults and organizations handling their records. Now, some of those details have ended up in the wrong hands. What I find especially troubling is how far back some of these records could go. Think about someone who left California years ago and has no reason to believe their old student information is still sitting on a testing company's system. That person could be living on the opposite side of the country and suddenly have to worry about a breach involving records from childhood. I appreciate that ETS is offering free identity protection, but I'd like to see schools and testing companies explain more clearly how long they keep sensitive student information and why. Parents deserve answers before a breach happens. Should schools and outside testing companies be allowed to keep sensitive student records for years after a child leaves, or should families have more control over when that information gets deleted? articles.title: Bipartisan pair of Senators press Kalshi, Polymarket over election markets
articles.summary: A bipartisan pair of senators are pressing Kalshi and Polymarket over prediction markets tied to the Nov. 3 midterm elections. “We write to express concerns about election-related prediction markets and to request specific information about your companies’ efforts to prevent insider trading, market manipulation, and wagers based on material nonpublic information,” Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.)…
articles.body:
A bipartisan pair of senators are pressing Kalshi and Polymarket over prediction markets tied to the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

“We write to express concerns about election-related prediction markets and to request specific information about your companies’ efforts to prevent insider trading, market manipulation, and wagers based on material nonpublic information,” Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and John Curtis (R-Utah) wrote in a letter addressed to Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour and Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan.

The senators were particularly concerned with “ election-related event contracts ” which are a type of asset class that gives users the ability to make trades about a specific yes or no question. It referenced several instances where candidates bet on their own races in 2025 and April 2026 on Kalshi, warning “these examples raise critical questions about how many election-related transactions have escaped detection.”

The letter also cited alleged market manipulation tactics on Polymarket during the 2024 presidential election affecting “roughly one-third of the presidential market’s trading volume,” according to one Fortune report .

A source from Kalshi said the company already “proactively” blocks candidates and staffers from trading on election markets using Federal Election Commission (FEC) payroll data as well as forming an independent market integrity committee to combat possible insider trading.

The senators asked both companies to provide the steps it had previously taken to prevent possible insider trading from campaigns and “other individuals with access to material nonpublic information” beyond using FEC filings. Their letter also asked what instances of election-related insider trading had been referred to the Commodities Futures and Trading Commission (CFTC) and what safeguards were currently in place.

“We remain skeptical that your companies can sufficiently police these even contracts with effective scrutiny and meaningful accountability,” the senators concluded.

The source added Kalshi looks forward to demonstrating how it keeps its platform free of insider trading.

Warren and Curtis’s letter follows up on Utah Attorney General Derek Brown (R) criminally charging Mansour along with other prediction market heads, alleging they illegally profited from promoting and offering online gambling within the state.

They face 13 felony counts and one misdemeanor count, according to a recent court filing.

In response to the letter, Kalshi’s head of enforcement Robert DeNault told The Hill, “Kalshi prohibits insider trading and market manipulation and proactively blocks candidates and campaign staff from trading to protect market integrity.”

“While fake polls have recently been promoted by major media outlets, our markets don’t lie—and have been largely non-reactive to fake information or attempts to distort the odds of candidates with big trades,” DeNault continued.

Polymarket did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: New World screwworm case reported in Arizona dog
articles.summary: Arizona reported its first case of New World screwworm on Wednesday, making it the third state to be impacted by the parasite. The confirmed case was found in a domestic dog in Cochise County, Ariz., which shares a border with Mexico, according to a press release from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The state’s Department…
articles.body:
Arizona reported its first case of New World screwworm on Wednesday, making it the third state to be impacted by the parasite.

The confirmed case was found in a domestic dog in Cochise County, Ariz., which shares a border with Mexico, according to a press release from the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

The state’s Department of Agriculture, which also confirmed the case in a Wednesday press release , noted the discovery was made when a veterinarian examined the dog on Oct. 26 and identified a maggot-infested wound on the animal’s back. Authorities conducted scientific testing, which verified the species.

“We have been preparing for this possibility for a long while and are acting swiftly,” State Veterinarian Ryan Wolker said in the release. “Because of the extensive outreach, coordination, and surveillance already in place, Arizona producers, veterinarians, and pet owners know what to look for and how to report suspected cases.”

The animal is under veterinary care, and the state’s department is working with the owner and the attending veterinarian to gather further information, according to the release.

“New World screwworm is a serious pest that affects livestock, pets, wildlife, and, less commonly, people,” the USDA release said. “The larvae feed on living tissue and can cause severe wounds, animal suffering, and significant economic impacts if not detected and treated quickly.”

The USDA has confirmed 71 cases of screwworm in three states — Texas, New Mexico and, most recently, Arizona. Out of those cases, 18 remain active as of Thursday. There is only one case that is associated with U.S. wildlife while the rest are in domestic animals.

The New World screwworm is a parasitic fly that can enter animals through open wounds and feed on living tissue. The first case of the flesh-eating parasite was reported in June in Zavala County, Texas.

articles.title: Trump administration’s definition of ‘medically frail’ unlawful, according to federal judge
articles.summary: A federal judge Thursday ruled that the Trump administration’s definition of “medically frail” used for Medicaid is unlawful, issuing a temporary injunction on states having to determine medical frailty. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns found in his ruling Thursday that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s definition of “medically frail” was “contrary to law” and…
articles.body:
A federal judge Thursday ruled that the Trump administration’s definition of “ medically frail ” used for Medicaid is unlawful, issuing a temporary injunction on states having to determine medical frailty.

U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns found in his ruling Thursday that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s definition of “medically frail” was “contrary to law” and that demands by plaintiff states to have it vacated were warranted.

The One Big Beautiful Bill passed last year included a new definition of “medically frail” that would exempt a Medicaid beneficiary from work requirements .

In order to be considered medically frail under the One Big Beautiful Bill, a beneficiary had to establish they had a “physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition” that “significantly” impaired their “ability to comply with the community engagement requirement.”

Prior to this, a person was considered medically frail if they met the Social Security definition of having a disability; had a substance use disorder; a disabling mental health condition; a physical, intellectual, or developmental disability that impaired their ability to perform basic activities or living; or a serious medical condition.

While the One Big Beautiful Bill did not eliminate these conditions, critics argued that having to also demonstrate a health condition “significantly impairs” a person’s ability to work was overly burdensome and threatened continued access to care.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) issued an interim final rule in June explaining to states how they should implement new Medicaid work requirements. The interim final rule limited the ability of states to rely on medical records to confirm medical frailty, only allowing them to use claims and encounter data from the 12 months preceding an application.

Critics argued that many patients who have been living with long-term or lifelong disabilities probably did not have a recent diagnosis confirming their disability.

Stearns agreed with plaintiff states’ argument that the 12-month rule was “arbitrary or capricious.”

“The States have met their burden of showing irreparable harm for which monetary damages would provide inadequate compensation – they face the burden of costly and intensive alterations to their eligibility verification system,” Stearns wrote.

The judge also issued a six-month stay on enforcement of states having to determine whether someone counts as medically frail, citing the short amount of time states have had to change their verification systems.

Medical groups welcomed news of the ruling Thursday.

“Today’s decision is a victory for patients as it strikes back against unnecessary barriers to care. The court rightly rejected a federal restriction that would have made it harder for people with serious or complex health conditions to qualify for an exemption from Medicaid work requirements,” Willie Underwood, president of the American Medical Association (AMA), said in a statement.

“Patients should not have to clear unnecessary bureaucratic hurdles to keep their health coverage, especially hurdles that go beyond what Congress intended,” said Underwood. “The AMA will continue fighting to protect access to medically necessary care and ensure bureaucratic red tape doesn’t stand in patients’ way.”

New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) said in a statement, “New Yorkers who are living with cancer, a disability, a serious mental health condition, or addiction should never have to prove they are sick enough to keep their health care. The more barriers to coverage there are, the less healthy our communities become. I am pleased to have secured this potentially life-saving relief for some of our most vulnerable New Yorkers.”

The Hill has reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.

articles.title: Elon Musk is ‘truly a genius,’ says Vladimir Putin
articles.summary: Putin said that he and Musk are in "close contact" about Rassvet, Russia's Starlink-like satellite connectivity project.
articles.body:
Russian president Vladimir Putin said that he and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk are in “close contact” about Rassvet , Russia’s answer to Starlink, Musk’s internet satellite service.

“Elon Musk is a genius, truly a genius,” Putin said at the Russia-Africa Summit on Wednesday. “He has already had more than 5,000 such satellites in orbit, while we are only taking the first steps.”

A potential relationship between Putin and Musk could have serious implications. Musk has recently voiced frustration with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whose country has been fighting a Russian invasion since 2022. After the U.S. eased sanctions on Russia earlier this month, Ukrainian officials became concerned that Ukraine could lose access to Starshield, the military version of Musk’s Starlink network, which Ukrainian forces rely on.

There was some merit to these concerns. For about 10 days earlier this month, Ukrainian drones experienced frequent losses of connectivity. According to the Wall Street Journal , Musk ordered SpaceX to limit Ukraine’s Starlink access, though other reports say the order came from the White House. Musk claimed in a post on X that Ukraine violated Starlink terms of service by using the technology for “offensive drone strikes to kill people.”

Starlink service in Ukraine appears to have since resumed normal operations.

“Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately,” Musk also wrote on X . “This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact.”

articles.title: Binance pauses withdrawals as hackers suspected of stealing billions in crypto | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Some estimates say hackers stole billions in crypto from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, during a cyberattack on Thursday.
articles.body:
Binance has confirmed to TechCrunch that it is dealing with a security incident as users reported that funds were being drained from the crypto exchange’s wallets.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch that it is “aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.”

“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement.

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”

Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary said that Binance has “temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks following a security incident as a precautionary measure.”

News of the breach comes hours after Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said in a post on X that the company had been likely hacked. Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered,” but did not provide an explanation for the claim.

Financial tech giant Circle froze about $800 million in Tether as it passed through its networks, while crypto giant Tether itself froze about $1.56 billion related to Binance’s hack.

Crypto watchers say at least $2 billion has been drained from Binance’s hot wallets, which are internet-connected cryptocurrency wallets that store crypto that are connected to the internet. By some estimates, Binance may have lost upwards of $5.7 billion in crypto , though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing.

It’s unclear who is behind the hack, and Binance did not say if it had received any correspondence from the hackers.

If confirmed into the billions, this would likely rank as one of the largest crypto breaches in history, according to leaderboards tracking crypto thefts.

In 2025, hackers stole a record $1.4 billion in crypto in a single breach from exchange Bybit, blamed on North Korean hackers.

In what appears to be a separate incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market giant Polymarket briefly halted trading after it confirmed that a third-party company was compromised, which led to the company pausing withdrawals. articles.body:
A suspected hack at Binance prompted cryptocurrency firms to freeze about $3 billion in assets, the company said on Thursday.

The exchange, which described the situation as a “security issue,” has temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while it “conducts security checks, freezes funds, and works with law enforcement.” It vowed to cover all losses.

“It does look like a hack on Binance,” the company’s co-founder Changpeng Zhao wrote in a post on the social platform X.

He touted fellow crypto firms Tether and Circle for quickly freezing funds. Zhao acknowledged he no longer manages the company but said he expects “all user funds will be fully covered.”

The Binance co-founder stepped down as CEO in 2023 when he pleaded guilty to violating anti-money laundering laws. President Trump pardoned Zhao in November 2025.

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his company froze more than $1.5 billion in USDT, the company’s dollar-backed stablecoin, in response to the potential hack. Stablecoins are digital tokens tied to stable assets, like the U.S. dollar.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire similarly said they are “closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance,” and have frozen more than $800 million in USDC associated with the incident. USDC is Circle’s stablecoin.

World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture launched by President Trump and his sons, froze $27 million of its USD1 stablecoin. Another crypto firm, Ripple, also said it was “actively freezing affected funds.”

articles.title: Wikipedia’s operator says a bad AI copyright ruling could threaten the open web
articles.summary: The Wikimedia Foundation filed an amicus brief urging a court to take a middle ground approach to fair use in a landmark AI copyright case.
articles.body: The Wikimedia Foundation is staking out a middle ground in a group of landmark AI copyright cases, pushing courts to legally protect large language models (LLMs) training on copyrighted work — but not chatbots regurgitating that work to users. An overly black-and-white ruling, it says, could either deprive Wikipedians of useful AI-based tools or endanger the open web. In an amicus brief filed Friday, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia weighed in on a set of lawsuits pitting publishers including The New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft, taking neither side. “Wikimedia is concerned that the parties’ positions in this case push for overbroad and simplified applications of the fair use doctrine” around AI, the organization says in its legal filing. A nuance-free victory for publishers, it fears, could let copyright holders “gatekeep” even innovative and transformative uses of their work. On the other hand, a victory for AI companies could constitute “a green light to snub licensing terms and fragment the flow of knowledge between human authors and audiences.” The ruling could be existential for Wikipedia. Wikimedia websites “have become one of the most critical sources of data for all artificial intelligence and machine learning training,” the company says in the filing. But these same systems siphon away visitors, undermining the communities that maintain these sites. Wikimedia argues that they’re also violating copyright: services like ChatGPT reproduce text that’s licensed freely under Creative Commons, it says, but don’t adhere to the terms of that license. At the same time, it says, the large language models that power these systems are useful to Wikipedia: they can help editors fight vandalism, detect copyright violations and doxxing, and look for articles that need improvement, among other uses. “A ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge, and stifle the development of open source technologies, ultimately impacting access to information for everyone in both cases,” Wikimedia Foundation general council Stephen LaPorte says in a statement. “The court needs to understand that Wikipedia is created through a collaborative process that requires a strong foundation of open and accessible human knowledge to thrive.” The Times argues for a more expansive definition of fair use as it applies to LLMs. It alleges, for example, that OpenAI infringed on its copyright by scraping its website to build training datasets. OpenAI and Microsoft both contend that using LLMs constitutes fair use. OpenAI has said that regurgitating work “is a rare bug.” Microsoft, in a September filing, says that expert analysis found that Copilot rarely reproduces full sentences from news content used to ground the model, which it said, “hardly undermines the transformative purpose of LLM training.” Wikimedia proposes a compromise. Scraping websites shouldn’t be considered copyright infringement, it argues, and using copyrighted works to pre-train LLMs without a license should constitute fair use when they provide “something new and different from the original sources,” according to a blog post. But if these models pull copies of material in response to user queries, then deliver it to users “while supplanting readers’ engagement with those original works,” that should require a license. The key difference is that in the latter case, AI output is simply substituting for the original work, and doesn’t transform it enough to qualify as fair use. In those cases, Wikimedia says that AI companies should respect licensing requirements to use such information. For Wikipedia, this would mean crediting the original source of information under its Creative Commons license, which also requires “any remix or adaptations” to remain under that same license. “We are taking a position in this case to defend the free and open human knowledge that Wikipedia depends on,” Wikimedia CEO Bernadette Meehan says in a statement. “Expanding access to knowledge through AI is a powerful goal, but it must respect the people, contributors, and communities that make reliable knowledge possible. Finding this balance is both a mutual benefit and a shared responsibility for the entire information ecosystem.”

articles.body: Hackers have stolen approximately $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what industry analysts are calling the largest cyber heist in digital asset history. The incident has again highlighted concerns regarding cybersecurity and the systemic risks of holding funds on centralised trading platforms. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis reported that the threat actors behind the coordinated attack originated from North Korea. According to TRM Labs, the attackers targeted Binance wallets across 10 distinct blockchains, siphoning the vast majority of the funds within an estimated 20-minute window.According to news agency Reuters, TRM Labs stated with “high confidence” that key characteristics of the intrusion closely mirror previous North Korean-sponsored operations, including a major 2025 cyberattack against cryptocurrency exchange Bybit that was formally tied to Pyongyang by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).Compromised laptop suspected as entry pointReuters reported that preliminary internal inquiries by Binance suggest the breach began through a single compromised endpoint. According to the exchange, unauthorised access was gained after an engineer’s laptop was hacked, allowing the attacker to infiltrate an internal network system and execute unauthorised fund withdrawals.“The incident stems from multiple factors. Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident,” Binance stated. Aravind Srinivasan, head of the systematic OTC business at cryptocurrency market maker GSR, described the unprecedented scale simply as “the biggest hack in history.”Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng to users: ‘Your money is safe’In response to the incident, Binance co-CEO Richard Teng posted a direct message on X for users to quell market panic and address solvency fears.I want to speak to you directly about what happened.Bottom line - your money is safe, and we're covering every loss.Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions.To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single "one-click" action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual.So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.We'll share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified - and publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete.What you need to know:• Your funds are safe• Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and company funds• Estimated total impact: ~$6.3B, with ~$3B frozen on-chain so far, in coordination with our blockchain partners• No evidence of any wallet private key leak• Deposits are unaffected and operating as normalWhat we've done:• Temporarily suspended withdrawals while we complete a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses• Revoked the affected address authorizations• Engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover fundsOur team hasn't stopped.
