articles.title: Backlash to AI data centers threatens GOP’s grip on Ohio, Texas
articles.summary: Salience around AI data centers is growing this election cycle as the fight over the infrastructure’s costs and environmental impacts may be threatening Republicans in battleground states like Texas and Ohio. Grassroots movements in rural communities, particularly where President Trump won by double-digit margins in each of his presidential bids, are threatening the rural vote…
articles.body:
Salience around AI data centers is growing this election cycle as the fight over the infrastructure’s costs and environmental impacts may be threatening Republicans in battleground states like Texas and Ohio.

Grassroots movements in rural communities, particularly where President Trump won by double-digit margins in each of his presidential bids, are threatening the rural vote the GOP has counted on for decades, experts and voters say.

The debate is emblematic in communities like Pickaway County, Ohio — which Trump won by around 50 points over former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 — where residents are airing their opinions on EdgeConneX’s latest data center.

“That’s weighing heavily, especially with the Senate races,” Pickaway County, Ohio, resident Sherri Fahringer, who is running for county commissioner, said regarding the data center issue.

Data centers are increasingly being built in rural communities, with 67 percent of planned projects slated in rural areas, according to an April Pew Research Center study.

Fahringer added that in the Ohio Senate race, the issue is pushing voters “further left toward” former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) in his campaign against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who has been knocked over his past support for data centers.

The League of Conservation Voters, along with other climate groups, have hammered Husted over his ties to data center projects — in one ad quipping that he “earned” the nickname, “the face of data centers.”

An August National Republican Senatorial Committee memo, first obtained by Axios , stated that Brown had made his opposition to data centers a “centerpiece of his campaign against Husted” because “it works.”

It also warned that “more than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

Trump won Ohio by over 10 points in 2024, but the GOP incumbent has trailed Brown in recent polling .

“It’s really fascinating because I know a lot of people who are opposed to data centers locally, and these are Republicans. Many of them are MAGA Republicans, very conservative areas,” Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and president of the advocacy group Alliance for Secure AI, said.

He noted that this debate differed from other issues, saying, “What makes this really powerful is you know this is a bipartisan coalition, and that’s kind of unique.”

A Bowling Green State University poll similarly found that opinions on data centers are the “one area many Ohioans share some common ground,” with 75 percent of respondents opposed to data center construction in their local communities and 78 percent favoring a moratorium on the construction of new data centers until further research can be done.

In Pickaway County, Fahringer says the bipartisan opposition has focused on projects’ expected impact on local energy grids and potential noise pollution, along with their locations.

“They’re being put on former farms right next to homes, very close to schools,” she said. “I think it is upending a lot of people’s typical votes that they would have you know, along party lines.”

The rural vote carries weight in Ohio, a state where all but five of 88 counties have more than 55 percent of their area classified as rural, according to an analysis by Cleveland.com using U.S. Census Bureau data.

“Rural areas are overwhelmingly Republican and conservative,” Steinhauser expressed. “You know, they went for the president by wide margins, but I think that a lot of those voters are concerned on this … they don’t support the president’s position here.”

Trump has repeatedly defended data center construction, arguing at a rally in Ohio that the projects were a boon to industry in the Buckeye State. More broadly, he has also taken a hands-off approach to regulation of AI development, of which data centers are central.

In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who is running for reelection and is a strong supporter of the president, has recently taken a different stance — proposing new restrictions on data centers in the state, including plans to set water-efficient technology requirements and repeal tax incentives. This comes after Abbott attempted to position Texas as the “ epicenter of AI development ” in 2025, when he announced new Google investments into data center projects.

Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller (R) told NewsNation , The Hill’s broadcast partner, that he believed GOP candidates could lose on Election Day because of data center development in Texas. He specifically called out Abbott for not taking a stronger stance against the projects.

“Basically, we’ve just quit listening to the people, and we’re gonna pay for it this election,” he said.

An October poll from the University of Texas and Texas Politics Project found that 66 percent of rural respondents opposed data center construction in their community, while 17 percent supported it.

Steinhauser, a Texas native, pointed to Abbott’s positioning on data centers as another “good barometer” for “where Texans are on a lot of issues, especially Republicans.” He added that the Texas governor “saw this movement” and adjusted.

Texas has the country’s largest rural population, a demographic Abbott’s opponent Gina Hinojosa (D) is hoping to court in her bid for the governor’s mansion. In the same poll, Hinojosa trailed behind Abbott among rural respondents, 28 percent to the incumbent’s 68 percent, but led overall by a single point — within the poll’s margin of error.

She has focused part of her campaign on attacking Abbott over data centers, saying in a New York Times interview that “rural Texas has felt betrayed” because of the governor’s actions around the AI infrastructure.

“Millions of voters in Texas alone are motivated by this right now, and it’s going to have an impact on the election,” Steinhauser remarked.

articles.title: Starlink drama puts spotlight on Musk’s global stature
articles.summary: Elon Musk and his business’s role in a recent dispute over Ukraine’s access to Starlink and its military network is putting a spotlight on the tech mogul’s outsized influence on the international stage. Following about 10 days of confusion and finger-pointing over what caused the slowdown of Starlink and its military-grade version — Starshield — in Ukraine, Musk acknowledged his company, SpaceX, was behind the restrictions on Starlink’s…
articles.body:
Elon Musk and his business’s role in a recent dispute over Ukraine’s access to Starlink and its military network is putting a spotlight on the tech mogul’s outsized influence on the international stage.

Following about 10 days of confusion and finger-pointing over what caused the slowdown of Starlink and its military-grade version — Starshield — in Ukraine, Musk acknowledged his company, SpaceX, was behind the restrictions on Starlink’s commercial services.

While the exact decision behind the specific Starshield slowdown is still contested, the debacle is underscoring the vast reach the world’s richest man has on global and military affairs.

“A lot of people are uncomfortable with the idea that an individual like a corporate leader, [is] essentially making foreign policy decisions about access, though it’s not clear what the alternative is in this case,” Michael Horowitz, director of the Defense and National Security program at the Council on Foreign Relations, told The Hill.

“This incident is a really good illustration of the absolutely vital role that Starlink and Starshield play in providing pretty unique capabilities that no other company or country can replicate,” he added.

Ukraine has used Starlink’s commercial services since the beginning of the Russia-Ukraine war and later added Starshield through SpaceX’s contract with the Pentagon.

The company provides internet service using its constellation of thousands of satellites. The distributed nature of Starlink’s architecture makes it more resilient than traditional military communications systems, noted Andrew Grotto, director of Stanford University’s program on geopolitics, technology and governance.

But Musk argued Saturday that using the commercial service “for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be.”

“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk wrote on X, the social media platform he owns.

Ukrainian officials disputed claims its military violated Starlink’s terms of service, arguing long-standing restrictions on the civilian system made offensive use impossible.

The SpaceX and Tesla CEO notably did not take responsibility for the Starshield outage, maintaining last Saturday that control of the military version, including decisions on speed, is up to the U.S. military and ultimately, the president. This is the same explanation Musk gave when Ukraine first reported the Starshield restrictions earlier this month.

In the days following the slowdown, Trump administration officials like Secretary of State Marco Rubio looked to deflect the controversial move , claiming Ukraine’s access to Starlink was up to Musk and not the White House.

The incident raised new questions and concerns about the tech mogul’s dominance in space and the U.S. military’s reliance on SpaceX following the incident in Ukraine.

Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) said last week he’s concerned both that U.S. national security is overly reliant on SpaceX and that Musk “has as much power as he does as one individual and one company over America’s ability to protect the domain of space, which is a warfighting domain.”

SpaceX, which was incorporated in 2002, is the largest satellite and space company, dominating the field and in turn, making Musk’s leadership even more important.

“No unelected civilian titan of industry should have the ability to interfere with a war in the way that SpaceX did here,” Grotto said.

“It’s never a good idea to concentrate a capability in a single point of failure,” he added. “And I think this episode highlights a real vulnerability, not just for Ukraine, but for the U.S. military more broadly.”

At the same time, the U.S. doesn’t have many alternatives. SpaceX’s main rival, Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, has struggled to make up ground.

“There’s not a really clear path for others to catch up,” said Armand Musey, president of the financial consulting firm Summit Ridge Group. “In order to compete with Starlink, you would need to have not only launch capacity, but batteries, processing, robotics, AI.”

Up until the last decade, Musey noted governments primarily “controlled the space sector” but now, “the script has been completely flipped.”

“Private sector folks, particularly SpaceX, really control the development of the sector and the government is sort of on the outside looking in,” added Musey, who focuses on space and satellite communications.

Looking back over the last century, “it’s hard to find a historical analogy for where an individual controlled something with such military importance,” said Sarah Kreps, director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University.

But she suggested there are some parallels with the Civil War, in which the Union was dependent on privately owned railroads and telegraph networks to move troops and supplies. President Lincoln ultimately intervened and took possession of the railroads for military purposes.

“What I think is different here is that the U.S. had jurisdiction over those railroads and the telegraph, and it doesn’t have jurisdiction over space necessarily,” Kreps noted. “And so that gives this one individual a significant influence over a foreign war.”

The Starlink controversy sparked scrutiny from Democrats and Republicans who questioned Musk’s role, and whether his relationship with the Trump administration played a part.

Musk became a key ally to Trump after spending heavily in the 2024 election, securing a short-lived role in the administration. Despite a public falling out with the president, the two appear to have largely reconciled over the past year.

While some may view the relationship between Trump and Musk with a wary eye, Kreps suggested there needs to be “coordination between his company and his decisions and U.S. priorities abroad.”

“I don’t think you want this private actor who has so much influence over the day-to-day operations of the war … just being a completely independent private actor,” she said.

She underscored the government also has levers of influence over Musk and SpaceX, including the company’s reliance on billions of dollars in federal contracts.

While Musk is aligned with the GOP, Musey argued political favoritism is not the driving force behind SpaceX’s dominance.

“Nobody can let him slow down because the effect of that is China would pull ahead,” Musey told The Hill, adding, “I don’t think the net effect would be that different under a Democratic administration.”

The latest controversy is not the first for Musk, who previously faced backlash over reports he reduced Ukraine’s capabilities on the battlefield. In one instance detailed in the biography, “Elon Musk,” by author Walter Isaacson, Musk single-handedly thwarted a Ukrainian raid by refusing to extend Starlink capabilities.

After first activating Starlink for free in Ukraine in 2022, it eventually became government-funded when the Pentagon signed a deal with SpaceX to provide Starlink’s commercial services to the embattled country. Ukraine added Starshield services in late 2024 through a Pentagon contract.

While Europe is exploring alternatives to Starlink with companies like Nokia and ICEYE, SpaceX’s satellite constellations are “in order of magnitude, larger than their competitors,” Horowitz said.

“It’s not like there’s a European option now Ukraine can switch to instead,” he added.

articles.title: Congress’ 65-year defense bill streak could be in jeopardy
articles.summary: Congress’ annual defense authorization bill is on shaky ground this year amid partisan infighting, threatening to upend the legislation’s unblemished 65-year streak of passage. The must-pass Pentagon policy bill, known as the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), is facing an uphill climb due to its historically high $1.15 trillion request — a figure that climbs…
articles.body:
Congress’ annual defense authorization bill is on shaky ground this year amid partisan infighting, threatening to upend the legislation’s unblemished 65-year streak of passage.

The must-pass Pentagon policy bill, known as the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), is facing an uphill climb due to its historically high $1.15 trillion request — a figure that climbs to $1.5 trillion should the Trump administration get its desired third reconciliation bill passed by Congress, also a tough climb.

Democrats feel the bill’s topline must be cut by hundreds of billions of dollars — and they want guardrails around Washington’s ongoing war against Iran — before they vote yes. That’s setting up a showdown with the Trump administration, which is not letting up on its desired dollar figure or close to a peace deal with Tehran that satisfies Democrats.

Mackenzie Eaglen, a defense budget expert at the American Enterprise Institute, said the distance between a “nightmare scenario,” in which the NDAA is not enacted, and the opposite, a defense bill bundle that includes a third reconciliation bill, is the widest gap she’s ever seen.

“The politics are absolutely dismal between the two branches right now,” she told The Hill.

She expressed fears that the NDAA would become increasingly difficult to pass if the streak is broken this year, as “we are living in a norm-shattering time of great disruption, including in politics.”

“Once red lines are crossed, it is difficult to go backward. I fear the necessary and bipartisan NDAA is fragile in this new era but hope I’m wrong,” Eaglen added.

The NDAA’s bumpy path was made clear in June when the House Armed Services Committee passed its version in a 44 to 12 vote, with an unusually small number of Democrats — half on the panel — voting in favor of the bill. Typically, only one or two Democrats on the historically bipartisan committee would oppose the bill as it heads to the House floor.

Then in July, the full House passed its NDAA by a narrow 216 to 212 vote, marking a departure from the broad bipartisan coalitions that have traditionally carried the defense legislation through Congress. A handful of Demcrats joined Republicans to pass the bill .

The Senate’s path has proved even more difficult. In July, senators failed to advance their version of the NDAA after a procedural vote of 50 to 46 , falling short of the 60 votes needed to succeed.

Democrats tanked it over concerns about top-line defense and non-defense spending levels. They also cited the then-resumption of the Iran war and Trump’s failure to ask Congress to authorize the conflict, which began on Feb. 28, as a major reason behind their opposition.

At the time, Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) called the Democratic vote to block the NDAA from coming up for debate “unprecedented.”

One defense industry expert with knowledge of deliberations over the bill said Republicans are likely to hold firm on the $1.15 trillion figure, a hill Democrats can use to extract numerous concessions in conference. But even with that give-and-take, the bill could still face a veto from President Trump.

“I think there’s a lot of things the Democrats will ask for, including possibly some language on Iran, but I think that it still becomes harder to pass,” they said.

As of late this month, House and Senate lawmakers are pursuing informal negotiations on a path forward.

The defense insider said Congressional staff have finished their work on the bill and unresolved issues have moved to the staff director level. The legislation is then to be taken up by the “Big Four” — the chair and ranking member of the House and Senate defense committees — once lawmakers come back to Capitol Hill after the November midterm elections. The goal is to have the bill completed by Thanksgiving, they said.

Another piece of the puzzle is the Pentagon’s push to have Congress formally authorize the agency’s name change from Department of Defense to “Department of War.”

The building’s top spokesman this week argued in favor of codifying the name change, with both the House and Senate Armed Services committees adopting measures in their draft bills that would do so.

Democrats, however, have called the switch unnecessary and accused the administration of engaging in semantics.

Other culture-war language in the bill could be dropped during negotiations, with language dealing with the conflict in Iran added in.

Most pressing is the war in Iran — the cost of which has gone up to $47 billion, an increase of more than $3 billion since last month — as Trump mulls launching strikes against Tehran after the U.S. midterm elections.

The Senate in September defeated a House-passed resolution directing Trump to withdraw U.S. troops from the conflict. But growing dissatisfaction among GOP senators over the president’s handling of the war, combined with the chamber possibly being overtaken by the Democrats after the midterms, marks a fresh chance to rein in the administration.

Lawmakers also appear determined to come together and get the bill over the finish line.

“It’s very important,” House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told Punchbowl News of the NDAA’s passage. “You know, we’re in very dangerous times. There’s a lot going on. We have to come together and get it done.”

Michael Herson, the president of lobbying firm American Defense International, predicted the process is going to be bumpy, “but it has been bumpy the last several years” and that the NDAA ultimately will be passed, keeping its streak in place.

“I haven’t given up hope on that,” he added.

articles.title: Private Equity Is Boosting Republicans Over Democrats in Midterms
articles.summary: The investing industry is throwing its weight behind Republican allies ahead of the US midterm elections in an effort to stem a populist wave it fears will b...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The investing industry is throwing its weight behind Republican allies ahead of the US midterm elections in an effort to stem a populist wave it fears will bring greater scrutiny of private equity's reach.

Private equity and money managers doled out more donations to Republicans than Democrats this year for the first time since 2016, with billionaires from Apollo Global Management Inc. and Blackstone Inc. opening their checkbooks. Blackstone's chief executive and Republican mega-donor Steve Schwarzman has donated more than $33 million to Republican candidates and their allies this cycle.

Overall, donations to Republican candidates, leadership political action committees and party committees from the investing sector were nearly 70% higher than comparable contributions supporting Democrats, according to OpenSecrets data.

That disparity in giving is far wider than has been seen in recent election cycles. But this year the industry has seen a rightward tilt amid concerns that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives – and maybe the Senate, too – and turn the spotlight on an industry that progressives have often cast as a bogeyman. The hope is to boost allies that could block regulation and serve as legislative brakes under Democratic control.

While they put dollars behind Republicans, credit executives have also stepped up visits to influential Democrats in recent months, said a person familiar with the matter. That includes meeting with Representative Maxine Waters, the person said, the ranking member on the House Financial Services Committee who is likely to take a bigger oversight role if the Democrats control the chamber.

Executives are not only girding for an unfavorable legislative agenda: They worry that the industry is poised for a moment like big bank CEOs faced in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, when executives were hauled in front of Congress for grilling. That kind of unwanted attention would be another headache for an industry already struggling with high interest rates, waning investor enthusiasm and underwhelming returns – and could come from a wide range of lawmakers.

"The industry views the populist streak on the right as just as worrying as the energy behind the progressive left," said James Maloney, managing partner of public affairs firm Tiger Hill Partners and a former spokesman for the industry's main lobby group.

articles.title: Binance hackers stole $6.3 billion in record-breaking crypto heist
articles.summary: Binance says $6.3 billion worth of crypto funds have been stolen from the platform, in what’s believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency hack on record.
articles.body: Binance has disclosed that $6.3 billion worth of crypto funds have been stolen from the platform, in what’s believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency hack on record. In a series of updates posted to X, the crypto exchange said that user funds are safe, and that around $3 billion of the impacted assets have been frozen so far. Binance has publicly committed to covering any losses resulting from the hack. The company has an emergency reserve fund of around $1.3 billion (at last valuation) to protect user assets in these situations, and said it has also reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident — $5 billion of which is “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.” “Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” Binance reported on X. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.” The company shared details about the compromised laptop that belongs to one of its DevOps engineers in a prior update, saying it allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Deposits and withdrawals have been suspended in response to the hack, and the affected address has had its authorization revoked. [Media: “To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions, and this was not a single ‘one-click’ action. It involved a more complex attack process,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. “Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.” Binance may not be pointing fingers at who’s behind the attack, but blockchain analysis firms TRM and Chainalysis both attribute it to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime hacking group that has a history of stealing funds from cryptocurrency exchanges. This is the largest known cryptocurrency heist in history— four times higher than the previous record, when $1.46 billion was stolen from Bybit last year — and according to TRM, most of the theft occurred over a period of just 20 minutes. [Media: This isn’t the first time Binance has been hacked, having suffered a previous security breach in 2019 in which $40 million worth of crypto assets (valued at the time) were stolen. The latest hack comes as cases of large-scale crypto theft are escalating, however, after several heists were disclosed by crypto companies in September. There are also new concerns around how AI tools can be used maliciously against the industry, with OpenAI reporting earlier this month that one of its models managed to swipe fake crypto on an Ethereum test network it didn’t have access to. “This is an extraordinary hack, for its size and for the response... Few financial systems have ever shown a theft of this scale,” TRM chief policy officer Ari Redbord said in a statement to Sky News. “The theft shows how exposed the system is to sophisticated attackers moving at a speed we have never seen.”

articles.title: North Korean hackers blamed for stealing record $6.3B in Binance breach | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Hackers working for North Korea are suspected of hacking a Binance employee's laptop, which allowed the theft of billions in crypto.
articles.body:
Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance . The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.

The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change.

In a post on X , Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”

Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto.

The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains.

Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”

Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners. The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.”

It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices.

Software is generally built from many components, including open source projects, which hackers regularly target , compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords, and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.

Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds.

Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.

Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.”

Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .

According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes.

Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million .

The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction.

articles.title: Slower wage growth curbs US labor costs in third quarter
articles.summary: By Lucia Mutikani WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - US labor costs increased moderately in the third quarter amid a slowdown in wage growth, suggesting that the...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - US labor costs increased moderately in the third quarter amid a slowdown in wage growth, suggesting that the labor market was unlikely to be an inflation risk.

The economy is struggling with rising price pressures, mostly stemming from the ‌ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran, which has raised the cost of energy goods and fertilizers, as well as an AI investment boom. ‌The Federal Reserve on Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." Economists expect the US central bank to raise borrowing costs in December.

"Labor-cost ​inflation continues to move in the right direction," said Priscilla Thiagamoorthy, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets. "While consumer inflation remains elevated, the Fed will take some comfort from the fact that the labor market is no longer a significant source of price pressures."

The Employment Cost Index (ECI), the broadest measure of labor costs, rose 0.8% last quarter after increasing 0.9% in the April-June period, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Friday. The increase in the ECI was in line ‌with economists' expectations.

Labor costs advanced 3.4% in the 12 ⁠months through September after rising by the same margin in the year through June. The ECI is viewed by policymakers as one of the better measures of labor market slack and a predictor of core inflation because it adjusts for ⁠composition and changes in job quality.

Wages and salaries, which account for the bulk of labor costs, climbed 0.7% last quarter after rising 0.9% in the second quarter. In the 12 months through September, wages increased 3.1%, mostly lagging inflation. They had advanced 3.2% in the year through June.

The government reported on Thursday that the Personal Consumption ​Expenditures ​price index shot up 3.6% year-on-year in September. Core PCE inflation, which excludes the volatile ​food and energy components, increased 3.1% on a year-on-year basis ‌in September. These two measures are tracked by the Fed for its 2% inflation target.

The BLS report showed wages adjusted for inflation dropped 0.6% in the 12 months through September after declining 0.3% in the year through June. Economists said this underscored what they called a cost of living crisis that was depressing consumer sentiment and tanking President Donald Trump's approval rating.

"Paychecks are barely able to keep workers' heads above water, trying to scratch out a living," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Bringing home a real paycheck that matches inflation is next to impossible for most Americans. No wonder consumer ‌confidence remains on the low side of life."

articles.title: Top Science Democrat probes cuts to research spending at National Science Foundation
articles.summary: A key Democrat is looking into a massive amount of money that was appropriated to the National Science Foundation (NSF) but reportedly not spent. In a letter first shared with The Hill, House Committee on Science, Space and Technology ranking member Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.) accused the foundation of violating “Congress’ power of the purse and…
articles.body:
A key Democrat is looking into a massive amount of money that was appropriated to the National Science Foundation (NSF) but reportedly not spent.

In a letter first shared with The Hill, House Committee on Science, Space and Technology ranking member Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.) accused the foundation of violating “Congress’ power of the purse and the rightful separation of powers in our constitutional system” after a report that 20 percent of its research budget went unspent in fiscal 2026.

Lofgren’s letter follows up on a New York Times report saying that the NSF withheld $1.4 billion appropriated by Congress for research. The Times reported, citing two people, that the Trump administration wants to redirect the money to priorities including AI and quantum computing.

The congresswoman also said NSF employees had told her staff the agency planned to spend the money that she later learned was repurposed.

“The agency told Committee Staff that it was behind schedule because of late appropriations, but that it had every intention of catching up on award-making by the end of the fiscal year,” she wrote.

“Subsequent reporting conveyed that NSF did not intend to distribute its full research budget to researchers across the country, but rather intended to divert a significant portion of its funding to advance unknown Trump Administration priorities,” she added. “For months, the most reliable source of information regarding NSF’s intentions for its research budget was the press, rather than the agency and the administration officials testifying about it before Congress.”

Lofgren, in her letter this week, asked the independent agency a series of questions including whether it intends to spend the money, how it is managing the funds and whether it received any direction from the White House.

While she holds limited investigative power now with Democrats in the minority, Lofgren stands to gain significant authorities, which she could use to further probe the issue, if her party takes back the House following next week’s midterms.

Democratic committee staff told The Hill that the oversight work they have been doing will continue into the next Congress.

A spokesperson for the science foundation said via email that it is “in receipt of the letter and will respond to Rep. Lofgren directly.”

As for the funding, the spokesperson said the agency “has carried over funds to invest in agency priorities that are aligned with broader Administration initiatives.”

“These funds have two-year availability under appropriations law and will be spent consistent with NSF’s congressional FY26 spending plan,” the person added. “NSF remains committed to investing in meritorious foundational research across the sciences and engineering that advances American scientific leadership.”

NSF is an independent agency that supports scientific research, primarily through grant funding. It supplies about a quarter of the federal support for research at U.S. universities.

Last year, anonymous staffers alleged that at the agency, “a covert and ideologically driven secondary review process by unqualified political appointees is now interfering with the scientific merit-based review system.”

articles.title: New federal rule requires drug intermediaries to disclose how they’re paid
articles.summary: The companies that manage billions of dollars in prescription drug spending for employers and workers will soon be required to inform their clients all the different ways they get paid under a new rule released by the Trump administration Thursday. A final rule by the Department of Labor will require pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) for…
articles.body:
The companies that manage billions of dollars in prescription drug spending for employers and workers will soon be required to inform their clients all the different ways they get paid under a new rule released by the Trump administration Thursday.

A final rule by the Department of Labor will require pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) for the first time to disclose detailed information about all their fees and compensation from drug manufacturers, pharmacies, consultants and more — which could help shed light on potential conflicts of interest.

PBM compensation has long been shrouded in secrecy and confidential agreements. The Labor Department said the new transparency could help employers negotiate contracts and seek lower prescription drug costs.

“This is a win for every American worker who has ever paid too much at the pharmacy counter,” Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said in a statement. “For years, PBMs have operated in the shadows, pocketing hidden fees while workers and employers were left in the dark. Today, President Trump is delivering the transparency Americans deserve – and putting American workers first.”

High prescription drug costs are a major concern to voters this election cycle, and the Trump administration has been promoting price transparency to reduce costs, though with minimal practical impact .

The final PBM rule is projected to save health plans and enrollees more than $800 million annually because of reduced prescription prices, the Department of Health and Human Services said. At most, the rule could save up to $22 billion over 10 years.

Still, transparency advocates and employer groups applauded.

“Large employers pay for their workers’ prescriptions, but many can’t see how much of that money their PBM and any affiliated entity keeps,” James Gelfand, president and CEO of the ERISA Industry Committee, said in a statement. “This rule changes that. Employers will be able to check the numbers, ask hard questions, and hold their vendors accountable to the contract.”

Pharmacy benefit managers are the intermediaries in the prescription drug supply chain that negotiate discounts with drug companies, paying pharmacies and determining which drugs patients can access and how much they cost.

They are often owned by and integrated into large insurance companies. The three biggest PBMs are UnitedHealth Group’s Optum Rx, CVS Health’s Caremark and Cigna’s Express Scripts, which represent about 80 percent of all U.S. prescriptions.

The rule will apply to self-insured employers, typically larger businesses that pay their own health claims. Implementation will begin on July 1, 2027. The rule enacts severe financial penalties and potential invalidation of the PBM contract if the companies don’t cooperate.

The PBM industry faced intense scrutiny on Capitol Hill last year; essentially every committee in both chambers with jurisdiction over healthcare drafted PBM reform legislation, and Trump also frequently railed against them.

Congress passed a law earlier this year to require PBMs to disclose more information. Officials said the law guided the drafting of the rule, with parts of the law to take effect after the rule does.

Critics say PBMs profit by steering people to more expensive drugs, driving up overall healthcare spending.

The rule was initially proposed in January and faced significant opposition from PBMs, health insurers and even some pharmaceutical companies.

David Marin, president and CEO of the PBM industry group Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, said the Department of Labor rule is “redundant” because Congress already enacted PBM transparency reform and called it “regulatory overreach” beyond the intent of Congress.

“[W]e are extremely concerned that it will lead to higher patient costs and less competition, the opposite of the Department’s stated intent,” Marin said in a statement. “Patients, employers, and unions will have no new meaningful transparency from this action, but prescription drug benefits will now be more expensive.”

articles.title: North Korea linked to $6.3B Binance hack
articles.summary: A North Korea-based cybercrime group appears to be behind a $6.3 billion hack of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, according to two blockchain intelligence firms. Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis tied the largest crypto hack on record to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit that has previously targeted the digital asset industry. Billions of dollars’ worth…
articles.body:
A North Korea-based cybercrime group appears to be behind a $6.3 billion hack of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance , according to two blockchain intelligence firms.

Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis tied the largest crypto hack on record to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit that has previously targeted the digital asset industry.

Billions of dollars’ worth of crypto began moving out of Binance wallets on Thursday afternoon. The company quickly suspended all deposits and withdrawals, and crypto firms froze about $3 billion in assets tied to the incident.

The attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on XRP Ledger, Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana and several other blockchain networks, with much of this occurring over the span of around 20 minutes, according to TRM Labs .

While the industry managed to freeze a significant portion of assets, the attacker still controls $2.4 billion “beyond any issuer’s reach,” the blockchain intelligence firm noted.

Chainalysis underscored that once the hack began, the attacker was “in a race against the clock” to swap out freezable assets, like USDT and USDC stablecoins, for nonfreezable assets, like Bitcoin and Ethereum.

“It was only a matter of time before the issuers of those stablecoins would freeze those funds,” it said.

Several aspects of the Binance hack match earlier North Korea-linked incidents, including a $1.5 billion hack of the crypto exchange Bybit last year, TRM Labs noted.

Binance has vowed to cover all losses associated with the incident. It said Friday morning that it has reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds for this effort.

“Difficult times like this are a great reminder of how strong our industry is when we work together,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said in a video posted to the social platform X. “We are grateful to our partners that acted quickly to freeze their assets, to global law enforcement who we are working with hand-in-hand to seek justice.”

“But most of all, we are grateful to our users for their patience and understanding,” he continued. “Rest assured that we are working nonstop to resolve this, to make the users whole and live up to their trust.”

articles.title: Meta settles with second plaintiff during trial over social media addiction
articles.summary: Meta settled a social media addiction lawsuit with an 18-year-old plaintiff on Friday, avoiding its next bellwether trial, which began jury selection this week. The case, filed by a woman from Mississippi dubbed “K.D.B.,” alleged her use of Instagram and Snapchat as a child worsened her mental health and contributed to her eating disorder, suicidal…
articles.body:
Meta settled a social media addiction lawsuit with an 18-year-old plaintiff on Friday, avoiding its next bellwether trial , which began jury selection this week.

The case, filed by a woman from Mississippi dubbed “K.D.B.,” alleged her use of Instagram and Snapchat as a child worsened her mental health and contributed to her eating disorder, suicidal thoughts, depression and self-harm.

K.D.B.’s case against Meta and Snap was consolidated with another plaintiff named S.J.’s claims against the company. Their legal teams argue the platforms intentionally designed their platforms to be addictive to young users.

In settling the case, Meta will avoid sitting through another high-profile trial during which CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, were expected to testify. Zuckerberg and Mosseri testified in previous trials over similar claims.

The trial will still move forward next week against Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, the plaintiffs’ attorneys confirmed.

Like K.D.B., S.J. is a teenager from Illinois who said she started using Snapchat at a young age, accessing features like “Snapstreaks” and “Snapscore” along with filters and push notifications.

Her suit alleges the features played a role in her compulsive use of Snapchat and contributed to her depression, eating disorder, anxiety and harm.

S.J. also settled her claims with Meta last week.

Emily Jeffcott, a Morgan & Morgan attorney representing K.D.B., said in a statement Friday the team remains “committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client.”

A spokesperson for Meta said “trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception.”

Jury selection began this week and continued Friday. Jury selection is expected to continue Monday and Tuesday, followed by opening arguments the next day. Snap CEO Evan Spiegel is expected to testify, which will mark his first trial testimony.

Snap did not comment on the settlement news Friday.

Ahead of the trial’s start earlier this week, a Snapchat spokesperson said the company was “built differently” from traditional social media platforms, arguing the claims “fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences” on the platform.

Snapchat “opens to a camera, not a feed, not a ranking of what other people post or other social comparison metrics,” the spokesperson said. “We have built safeguards into the platform, introduced safety tools and educational resources, and we believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first.”

In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement for similar claims, ending a high-profile trial that was already underway in California. The settlement involved 47 U.S. states, three territories and the District of Columbia after Meta said it approached “nearly every state” to collaborate on a safety framework.

Meta also agreed to pay Texas more than $1 billion over similar allegations .

Along with the payments, the company also agreed to set default daily time limits of two hours for users younger than 18 that can only be lifted by a parent, and it introduced blocks during the nighttime and blocked notifications during school hours.

Meta’s spokesperson touted this agreement in a statement Friday. “We’ve spent more than a decade building protections for teens,” the spokesperson said, adding, “We hope the rest of our industry joins us in setting this new standard.”

articles.title: Rates need to be higher, 3 Fed members say. The question is how much.
articles.summary: Three Fed officials spoke Friday about the need for further hikes in the face of high inflation.
articles.body:
Three members of the Federal Reserve suggested Friday that interest rates need to move higher to push down inflation.

St. Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem said he thinks inflation is too high and broad-based, and that the Fed needs to act "soon," otherwise higher prices will persist.

"I judge that additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon," Musalem said in a speech in New York.

Hiking now, he said, will do less harm to the economy than if inflation becomes entrenched.

"Incremental adjustments made earlier are usually less disruptive than larger and abrupt actions taken later," said Musalem. "Moving sooner in smaller steps while inflation expectations are anchored has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or economic growth."

In a speech in North Carolina on Friday, Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan reiterated that she believes the Fed needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases before pausing to re-evaluate.

"I currently estimate that the fed funds target range is at least 50 basis points — half a percentage point — below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target," Logan said.

"Adjusting policy more gradually can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary," Logan said.

Elsewhere, Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin also suggested that the central bank needs to raise rates further to bring down inflation in the face of strong demand. The question is by how much.

"What you see is inflation's high, demand's solid, unemployment's relatively low, and so I think the direction of travel is pretty straightforward," Barkin said in an interview with SiriusXM Business Radio. "I think the question though is pace."

Barkin noted that Fed officials have signaled taking a gradual approach to raising rates.

"Gradual makes sense when you're not much behind the curve where you want time to learn, both from the economic environment and the external environment, and so we haven't seen much change since then," he said. "We'll see what we learn over the next period of time."

The Fed voted in a split decision this week to hold rates steady even as inflation has moved higher. A day later, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up in September , solidifying expectations for an interest rate hike in December. The Personal Consumption Expenditures index rose 3.6%, up from 3.4% a month earlier. On a core basis, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, PCE rose 3.1%, up a tenth of a percentage point from 3% in August. Month over month, core PCE clocked in at 0.3%, in line with projections, but marking a faster pace from the 0.2% seen in August.

articles.title: Navy airman recounts USS Lincoln leap: ‘If I was supposed to die then I would have just been dead’
articles.summary: One of the eight sailors who attempted suicide by jumping overboard during the grueling deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier strike group is speaking out after he was effectively punished for the incident. Navy airman Nicholas McKelvey, 19, jumped overboard on Aug. 3, 255 days into the ship’s deployment, The New York Times…
articles.body:
One of the eight sailors who attempted suicide by jumping overboard during the grueling deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier strike group is speaking out after he was effectively punished for the incident. Navy airman Nicholas McKelvey, 19, jumped overboard on Aug. 3, 255 days into the ship’s deployment, The New York Times reported . McKelvey, an aviation mechanic in a helicopter squadron, told the outlet he had been working 12-hour shifts on the flight deck in extreme heat with limited food , had missed the birth of his daughter and was dealing with in-laws battling cancer when he hit his limit and jumped into the Arabian Sea. U.S. Navy records reviewed by the Times said he was rescued by a helicopter crew and returned to the ship 50 minutes later, with a report on the incident seeming skeptical of what caused him to take the leap. In the report, an officer acknowledged that it had been “a difficult deployment” and that “it is unsurprising that we might have a jumper.” But they also said McKelvey’s “motives are undetermined” and “the conditions in which he jumped appear suspect,” pointing to the fact he wore his “float coat,” a vest that can be used as a flotation device. “I didn’t want to be there anymore,” the airman told the Times. “If I was going to die because of it, then that’s just how it is.” He later added: “Obviously, I was trying to get home. I kept my float coat on because if I wasn’t supposed to die then I was going to get saved , but it didn’t matter, and if I was supposed to die then I would have just been dead. It’s that simple.” The Navy on Thursday moved to discharge McKelvey, accusing him of faking a mental health crisis to end his deployment, making him ineligible for education assistance under the GI Bill of Rights. The Lincoln earlier this month docked in San Diego, completing its 322-day deployment, which was expected to end this summer but was extended as part of the war against Iran. The aircraft carrier had helped enforce the U.S. naval blockade in the region. The deployment has come under intense scrutiny due to the tight food supplies and degrading mental health on board the massive ship and its strike group. The Lincoln did not have a port call for 286 days until it finally docked in Thailand for a short period last month. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao later revealed there had been eight suicide attempts during the lengthy deployment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has conceded the Lincoln’s crew members operated in a tough environment but accused the news media of attempting to “turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale, or a symbol of a failed mission.” But McKelvey and his wife, Samantha Larry, said they are speaking out now because they believe he received inadequate mental health care before and after his jump, making his punishment unfair. The sailor said in June that he visited the ship’s medical unit for mental health care but was directed to speak with a chaplain, a choice he declined, according to the Times. The Lincoln only had six mental health specialists for a ship of more than 5,000 service members. “They don’t want to take accountability for what happened to him, and to what happened to multiple sailors on the boat,” Larry said about her husband. “I don’t think that they care.” She added, “They care more about how they’re pictured, how they’re viewed. They don’t want anyone to see the bad stuff.” The Navy charged McKelvey with malingering and “absence without leave” for abandoning his post when he jumped, according to the charging papers, reviewed by the outlet.

One of the eight sailors who attempted suicide by jumping overboard during the grueling deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier strike group is speaking out after he was effectively punished for the incident.

Navy airman Nicholas McKelvey, 19, jumped overboard on Aug. 3, 255 days into the ship’s deployment, The New York Times reported .

McKelvey, an aviation mechanic in a helicopter squadron, told the outlet he had been working 12-hour shifts on the flight deck in extreme heat with limited food , had missed the birth of his daughter and was dealing with in-laws battling cancer when he hit his limit and jumped into the Arabian Sea.

U.S. Navy records reviewed by the Times said he was rescued by a helicopter crew and returned to the ship 50 minutes later, with a report on the incident seeming skeptical of what caused him to take the leap.

In the report, an officer acknowledged that it had been “a difficult deployment” and that “it is unsurprising that we might have a jumper.” But they also said McKelvey’s “motives are undetermined” and “the conditions in which he jumped appear suspect,” pointing to the fact he wore his “float coat,” a vest that can be used as a flotation device.

“I didn’t want to be there anymore,” the airman told the Times. “If I was going to die because of it, then that’s just how it is.”

He later added: “Obviously, I was trying to get home. I kept my float coat on because if I wasn’t supposed to die then I was going to get saved , but it didn’t matter, and if I was supposed to die then I would have just been dead. It’s that simple.”

The Navy on Thursday moved to discharge McKelvey, accusing him of faking a mental health crisis to end his deployment, making him ineligible for education assistance under the GI Bill of Rights.

The Lincoln earlier this month docked in San Diego, completing its 322-day deployment, which was expected to end this summer but was extended as part of the war against Iran. The aircraft carrier had helped enforce the U.S. naval blockade in the region.

The deployment has come under intense scrutiny due to the tight food supplies and degrading mental health on board the massive ship and its strike group. The Lincoln did not have a port call for 286 days until it finally docked in Thailand for a short period last month.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao later revealed there had been eight suicide attempts during the lengthy deployment.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has conceded the Lincoln’s crew members operated in a tough environment but accused the news media of attempting to “turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale, or a symbol of a failed mission.”

But McKelvey and his wife, Samantha Larry, said they are speaking out now because they believe he received inadequate mental health care before and after his jump, making his punishment unfair.

The sailor said in June that he visited the ship’s medical unit for mental health care but was directed to speak with a chaplain, a choice he declined, according to the Times.

The Lincoln only had six mental health specialists for a ship of more than 5,000 service members.

“They don’t want to take accountability for what happened to him, and to what happened to multiple sailors on the boat,” Larry said about her husband. “I don’t think that they care.”

She added, “They care more about how they’re pictured, how they’re viewed. They don’t want anyone to see the bad stuff.”

The Navy charged McKelvey with malingering and “absence without leave” for abandoning his post when he jumped, according to the charging papers, reviewed by the outlet.
